cases.title: Acute limb ischaemia
cases.stem: A patient presents with sudden severe leg pain, coolness and progressive sensory loss. CTA shows an acute femoropopliteal occlusion.

questions.question: Which clinical feature most increases the urgency of revascularisation?
questions.explanation: Neurological deficit indicates threatened limb viability and requires urgent revascularisation.

questions.question: In a threatened but salvageable limb, which endovascular option may provide rapid thrombus removal in selected patients?
options: Observation for several weeks without anticoagulation
questions.explanation: Percutaneous thrombectomy can rapidly restore flow in appropriate anatomy and clinical settings.

questions.question: Which factor strongly argues against catheter-directed thrombolysis?
questions.explanation: Recent major intracranial intervention confers a high risk of catastrophic bleeding.

questions.question: After thrombus removal, a severe underlying stenosis is demonstrated. What should be done?
options: Assess and treat it when it is the likely cause and treatment is technically appropriate
Embolise the distal artery with particles
questions.explanation: Treating the underlying causal lesion may reduce the risk of immediate or recurrent thrombosis.

questions.question: After successful revascularisation of a severely ischaemic limb, which complication requires active surveillance?
questions.explanation: Reperfusion can produce tissue oedema and compartment syndrome after prolonged limb ischaemia.

cases.title: Percutaneous biliary drainage
cases.stem: A patient has cholangitis due to malignant hilar obstruction. Endoscopic drainage has failed and percutaneous drainage is requested.

questions.question: What is the principal indication for percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage in this setting?
options: Decompress an obstructed biliary system when endoscopic drainage is not feasible or has failed
questions.explanation: Percutaneous drainage is an established route for biliary decompression when endoscopic management is not possible or unsuccessful.

questions.question: Which factors should be reviewed before puncture?
options: Biliary anatomy, coagulation status and relevant ascites
questions.explanation: Anatomical planning and bleeding/infection risk are central to safe percutaneous access.

questions.question: When the biliary system is infected, which procedural principle is important?
options: Achieve effective drainage while avoiding unnecessary high-pressure contrast injection
Inject repeated large-volume contrast boluses under pressure
questions.explanation: Overpressurising an infected system may promote bacteraemia and sepsis; decompression is the priority.

questions.question: Which is a recognised complication of percutaneous biliary drainage?
questions.explanation: Bleeding and infection/sepsis are important complications of transhepatic biliary intervention.

questions.question: After successful biliary decompression for cholangitis, what is an appropriate immediate management principle?
options: Ensure effective external/internal drainage and monitor for sepsis or haemorrhage
Inject large volumes under pressure to prove patency
Remove the catheter before clinical improvement
questions.explanation: Effective low-pressure drainage and close monitoring are central after decompression of an infected biliary system.

questions.question: A type I endoleak after EVAR represents:
options: Failure of seal at a proximal or distal attachment zone
Retrograde filling from lumbar arteries only
questions.explanation: Type I endoleak is a high-pressure sealing failure and usually requires correction.

questions.question: A type II endoleak is typically caused by:
options: Retrograde flow from branch vessels such as lumbar arteries or the inferior mesenteric artery
Proximal graft migration in every case
questions.explanation: Collateral branch vessels can maintain retrograde flow into the aneurysm sac.

questions.question: For a suitable post-catheterisation femoral pseudoaneurysm, a common percutaneous treatment is:
questions.explanation: Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection is highly effective in appropriately selected pseudoaneurysms.

questions.question: Which is an important relative contraindication to percutaneous biopsy?
questions.explanation: Coagulopathy increases haemorrhagic risk and should be optimised whenever possible.

questions.question: Pre-treatment angiographic planning for hepatic radioembolisation is primarily used to:
options: Identify extrahepatic branches and assess hepatopulmonary shunting
questions.explanation: Planning helps prevent non-target microsphere deposition and quantify lung shunt.

questions.question: An intraprocedural advantage of cryoablation is:
options: The ice ball can be visualised on imaging
Pain is absent in every patient
Adjacent structures do not need monitoring
questions.explanation: Visualisation of the ice ball helps assess the ablation zone and relationship to adjacent structures.

questions.question: Ultrasound guidance for central venous access primarily reduces:
options: The need for tip-position assessment when indicated
questions.explanation: Real-time ultrasound improves first-pass success and reduces mechanical complications.

questions.question: The best way to reduce non-target embolisation is to use:
options: Selective catheterisation, careful angiographic mapping and flow control
questions.explanation: Precise vascular mapping and controlled delivery are essential to minimise non-target embolisation.

questions.question: A haemodynamically stable patient has a contained iatrogenic common femoral artery perforation after angioplasty. Which endovascular option may be considered when anatomy is suitable?
questions.explanation: A covered stent can seal an arterial perforation while maintaining vessel patency in selected anatomy.

questions.question: During vertebral augmentation, which complication is specifically related to cement injection?
options: Cement leakage with possible neural or venous consequences
Portal vein thrombosis in every patient
questions.explanation: Cement extravasation is a procedure-specific risk of vertebral augmentation.
